Biology plays a role: testosterone tends to nudge desire upward in both sexes, and very low levels in men or women are linked to lower libido. But averages are not destinies. Imagine two hills that overlap: the “male” hill is shifted a bit higher for desire, yet there’s a wide shared middle. Plenty of women have stronger drives than many men, and individual differences are huge.

Context also matters—a lot. Desire is more like a set of sliders than a single on/off switch: stress, sleep, mental health, relationship quality, medications (like antidepressants), and life stages can move those sliders. Women’s desire can shift across the menstrual cycle, after childbirth, or around menopause; men’s desire often declines slowly with age or illness. Culture shapes reporting, too: norms that encourage men to be forward and women to be reserved can inflate the apparent gap.

So, there is a small-to-moderate average difference favoring men, but the overlap is large, and situation and culture can widen or narrow it. For any one person or couple, it’s better to think “what turns our particular dials?” than “what usually happens by sex.”

Think of a busy road as a fast, unpredictable river that suddenly appeared in the landscape about a century ago. Natural selection is the slow sculptor that improves swimmers generation by generation—if they survive to have young. In that short window, some quick‑breeding species have shown hints of change that make them better at dodging cars. One well‑studied example is cliff swallows nesting on highway bridges in the United States: over a few decades, the population near roads evolved shorter wings, which makes them more agile and less likely to be hit. Some birds also now take off sooner when a car approaches, and certain animals time their crossings for quieter hours. These shifts can come from learning within a lifetime, culture passed from parent to young, or, in a few cases, inherited traits favored by survival.

But for many animals—especially large, long‑lived ones like deer, foxes, and owls—a hundred years is only a handful of generations. For them, cars are a new “predator” that kills indiscriminately, often before natural selection can improve road‑crossing skills. The result is that roadkill remains common and roads fragment habitats. Where we do see clear improvements in survival, the biggest gains usually come from our actions: wildlife overpasses and underpasses, fencing that guides animals to safe spots, lower night‑time speed limits, and better roadside design. So the short answer is “a little, in some species,” but the most reliable way to help animals cross the road isn’t waiting for evolution—it’s building safe bridges over that fast river we created.

Think of the International Space Station as a submarine in space: it can’t open a window, so it recycles its air. Solar power runs an “oxygen factory” that splits water into oxygen and hydrogen, much like artificial gills. The oxygen is fed into the cabin for the crew to breathe. The carbon dioxide they exhale is pulled out by air filters, and much of the leftover hydrogen is then combined with that carbon dioxide in another device to make water again. This closes a big part of the loop: water becomes oxygen, breath becomes carbon dioxide, and some of that becomes water again, ready to be split once more.

The loop isn’t perfect, so the station still needs top-ups. Cargo ships regularly deliver water and gas, which are far easier and safer to haul than big tanks of oxygen alone. There are two main oxygen-making systems—one on the U.S. side and one on the Russian side—plus backups: stored gas tanks and “oxygen candles” that release oxygen when heated for emergencies. Plants on board make only a tiny amount, more for science than supply. By recycling as much as possible and resupplying the rest, the station keeps a steady, breathable atmosphere day after day.

For an individual snake, the number of vertebrae is set before it hatches or is born and does not increase as it grows. Think of a snake’s backbone like a train built in the factory: the number of cars is decided during construction. After the train leaves the station (birth), the cars don’t get added; they just get bigger and stronger. Snakes lengthen by enlarging their existing vertebrae and the soft tissues between them, not by making new vertebrae.

What isn’t fixed is the count across all snakes. Different species—and even different individuals of the same species—can have different totals, ranging from roughly 150 to well over 400 vertebrae, with some forming the body and the rest the tail. Factors during early development, such as incubation conditions, can nudge the final count a little, but by the time the snake hatches, it’s locked in. Later in life, bones may fuse or be damaged, which can change how the backbone looks, but new vertebrae are not added. So each snake keeps the same number it started with, even as the “train cars” grow.

Snakes don’t add new ribs or vertebrae as they get longer. The total number is set very early, while the embryo is forming, and it stays the same after hatching or birth. As a snake grows, each vertebra and its attached rib simply get bigger, not more numerous—think of a train that keeps the same number of cars, but each car stretches and strengthens as the train matures. In most snakes, ribs are attached to nearly every body vertebra in the trunk (not on the first couple in the neck and not on the tail), which is why their whole body seems “ribbed.”

How many vertebrae a snake has depends on the species and is decided during development when the embryo lays down the body in repeating blocks of tissue—like sewing a long line of identical quilt squares. Some species “sew” 150 squares, others 300 or more, which is why adult lengths and body shapes vary so much among snakes. There can be small individual differences within a species, but once the pattern is set in the embryo, the blueprint is locked: no new squares, just bigger ones as the animal grows.

Because a nuclear blast is mostly a wave of crushing air and intense heat, setting it off a short distance above the ground spreads those effects over a much larger area. Picture the fireball as a glowing sphere. If it goes off on the ground, half of that sphere is buried in dirt and rock, wasting energy digging a hole. If it goes off in the air, the whole sphere can “look down” on the city. The shock wave races outward, then bounces off the ground and merges with the incoming wave, giving everything near the surface a double hit. It’s like slapping a pond from just above the surface: you get a wide, strong ripple. Slap from under the water and much of your effort just churns mud. An air burst also lets more of the blinding heat travel in straight lines, igniting more fires over a broader area.

There’s another practical reason: fallout. A ground blast sucks huge amounts of soil into the fireball, turns it radioactive, and drops it back down as dangerous dust. Detonating in the air picks up far less dirt, so nearby fallout is reduced, even though the immediate blast and heat damage are worse over a wider region. There are exceptions: if the goal is to crack bunkers or collapse tunnels, a ground or underground burst is chosen despite the extra fallout, because you want to shove energy into the earth. But for “soft” surface targets, an air burst is the way to turn one explosion into the widest “umbrella” of pressure and heat.
